title: 3-Read Friday #86: Securing Attention, Definitions, and the Post-Literate Society
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #86 moves from classroom-level attention to assessment design to a sweeping civilisational argument. Shaun Allison shares practical steps for maintaining attention once a teacher has secured it, distilled from a departmental planning session at Durrington. Matthew Evans argues that definition questions are informationally poor and proposes contrast, sorting, multiple-choice, extraction, and correction questions as richer alternatives for probing conceptual understanding. James Marriott closes the issue with a wide-ranging essay on declining reading and its implications for cognition, culture, and democracy, which Barton flags as the least optimistic but most powerful piece of the three. Barton's framing moves the issue from the granular (a teaching technique) to the civilisational (what a post-literate society loses).
points: Allison's piece distils an actual departmental planning session at Durrington into concrete techniques -- least invasive intervention, explanations punctuated with questions, storytelling, voice variation, and "Pastore's Perch" -- for maintaining, not just securing, attention.

Evans' argument reframes assessment design around information yield: a definition question tells you little about whether a student understands a concept's boundaries, while contrast and sorting questions expose whether they can distinguish examples from non-examples.

Marriott's essay is explicitly the issue's outlier in scope and tone -- Barton flags it as "not the most optimistic" of the three picks, tying declining literacy to broader claims about attention, democracy, and cultural stagnation.

Read together, the three picks trace a throughline from classroom technique (Allison) to assessment design (Evans) to the civilisational stakes of literacy itself (Marriott), moving from the granular to the sweeping across the issue.
quotes: Many schools I visit use things like narrated countdowns to focus students’ attention. This is all well and good, but how do we then maintain that attention?
I have considered definitions a tad overrated for a while now. Sure, students can parrot back the definition of a polygon or a quadratic equation, but do they understand what it actually means?
I wouldn’t describe this as the most optimistic of posts, but it is certainly a powerful one.
James cites evidence about the decline in reading in general, the changing nature of the books we do read, and the implications for humanity. Spoiler alert: they are not good.
In this post, Matthew shares some tests of conceptual understanding that go beyond recall of a definition.
